top.title: TCU fires football coach Sonny Dykes, per reports
top.description: Four years after leading the Horned Frogs to within one win of a national championship, Sonny Dykes is out as TCU's football coach. (LM Otero/AP Photo/LM Otero) TCU has fired head football coach Sonny Dykes , according to multiple reports Sunday. Dykes was dismissed after a 38-17 loss to No. 2 Utah on Saturday that dropped the Horned Frogs to 5-6 and 3-5 in the Big 12. Since reaching the College Football Playoff championship game in 2022, TCU has gone 28-21. Dykes is the second Big 12 coach to be fired this season, joining Baylor's Dave Aranda. It was not immediately known if Dykes will coach the Horned Frogs in Thursday's regular-season finale at Texas Tech. Dykes went 41-23 in his five seasons at TCU, with his first year being the high-water mark, a 13-2 campaign that included the school's first berth in the CFP (when the field was four teams) and a victory over Michigan in the semifinals before a blowout loss to defending national champion Georgia in the title game. Prior to his time at TCU, Dykes coached five years at SMU (30-18), four seasons at Cal (19-30) and three years at Louisiana Tech (22-15). Dykes, the son of legendary former Texas Tech coach Spike Dykes, also was an assistant at his alma mater Tech as well as Kentucky, Arizona, Northeast Lousiana and Navarro College. top.title: Camara to continue with Haas for final two races
top.description: It was announced in October that Rafael Camara will be joining Haas for the 2027 season [Getty Images] Brazilian Rafael Camara will continue to race for the Haas team for the final two grands prix of the Formula 1 season. The 21-year-old, who was already signed to drive for the US-based team in 2027 , was drafted in for this month's Sao Paulo Grand Prix after Frenchman Esteban Ocon was dropped following a bust-up with team boss Ayao Komatsu. The decision to keep Camara in the Haas seat in preparation for next season means he will likely lose the Formula 2 title. He is leading the F2 championship by seven points from Bulgarian Nikola Tsolov heading into the final two events in Qatar and Abu Dhabi. Komatsu said: "We're excited to be able to finish the season with Rafa driving and build on his first two race starts with the team in Brazil and America. "I'm delighted that Rafa's embraced every track session as a learning opportunity and embedded himself further within the team. "We now get to finish the season together which is advantageous to us all ahead of a relatively short off-season and as our 2027 preparations get under way." A statement from Haas announcing the move did not include a quote from Camara. top.title: PSG plan to sign new forward in winter to compensate injury absences
top.description: PSG plan to sign new forward in winter to compensate injury absences Paris Saint-Germain have seen their autumn take a nightmarish turn. Having already been assured that they would be without Kvicha Kvaratskhelia (25) for several months following a torn anterior cruciate ligament in his right knee sustained against FC Barcelona in late October, the reigning double European champions suffered a further blow on Saturday when Désiré Doué (21) sustained the same injury during the Parisians’ away match at Nice. These are two massive setbacks for the Red and Blues, whose aim of winning the Champions League for the third consecutive season has inevitably taken a serious knock. And in an attempt to keep their hopes of a remarkable feat alive, the Parisian management intend to make the most of the upcoming winter transfer window to strengthen the squad. As reported by Le Parisien , several attacking players are reportedly under consideration. These are players with clearly defined characteristics and a versatile profile – primarily wingers – capable of unbalancing defences and winning one-on-one duels, as well as being comfortable in tight spaces. Whilst the exact identities of the targeted players have not been revealed, neither AS Monaco’s Paris Brunner (20) nor AFC Bournemouth’s Eli Junior Kroupi (20) are believed to feature in the plans of Luis Campos, with the Parisian sporting director seeking to invest sensibly, without splashing the cash. top.title: Cleveland Browns: Run game has a chance to get rolling after the bye
top.description: (Photo by Lauren Leigh Bacho/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Cleveland Browns have struggled on offense in several areas this season, and the rushing game is no exception. As the Browns use the bye week to rest up for the final seven games of the season and a potential playoff run, the numbers from the run game are not pretty. Running back Quinshon Judkins leads the team with a meager 423 rushing yards, followed by quarterback Deshaun Watson with 266. Judkins is averaging just 3.4 yards per rush, not exactly what you want to see from your top running back, and has six games with fewer than 50 rushing yards. It’s not all Judkins fault, of course, as the offensive line has taken time to coalesce with five new starters, and opposing defenses are not exactly afraid of the pass game, which makes it that much harder to run the ball. The good news is that the final seven games provide ample opportunity for the Browns to get the run game in gear as they will face some of the league’s worst run defenses. Let’s run through the teams the Browns will be facing to see where they currently rank* when it comes to stopping the run: Week 12 vs. Las Vegas: 1,511 rushing yards (ranked No. 31) and 13 rushing touchdowns allowed (tied for No. 21) Week 13 & 18 vs. Cincinnati: 1,115 rushing yards (ranked No. 20) and 8 rushing touchdowns allowed (No. 16) Week 14 vs. Atlanta: 1,191 rushing yards (ranked No. 26) and 10 rushing touchdowns allowed (tied for No. 18) Week 15 vs. New York Giants: 1,094 rushing yards (ranked No. 18) and 7 rushing touchdowns allowed (tied for No. 11) Week 16 vs. Baltimore: 1,059 rushing yards (ranked No. 15) and 14 rushing touchdowns allowed (tied for No. 30) Week 17 vs. Indianapolis: 1,478 rushing yards (ranked No. 30) and 10 rushing touchdowns allowed (tied for No. 18) As the weather starts to turn colder, the Browns are going to need their running game to function at a higher level if they hope to stay in the playoff race in the AFC. The schedule is set up well for them to accomplish that goal, which would also help open up the passing game and provide the “explosive plays” that have been missing for most of the season. Accomplish that, and the playoff dreams just might turn into playoff reality. *Stats are heading into Week 11’s slate of games. Bring the Dawg Pound with you on the SB Nation app! top.title: How skipping shootaround helped the Spurs beat New Orleans
top.description: San Antonio Spurs guard De'Aaron Fox (4) drives down the court during an NBA game against the New Orleans Pelicans at Frost Bank Center in San Antonio, Saturday, Nov. 21, 2026. (Sam Owens/San Antonio Express-News) De'Aaron Fox wandered into the Spurs' locker room late Saturday night after a 114-91 victory over New Orleans , trying his best to stifle a yawn. He failed miserably. In the midst of the busiest month on the Spurs' schedule, Fox was hardly alone in feeling the effects of a long NBA grind. "When you've been through this for a few years, you get used to the course of an NBA season," Fox said. "There's no excuses. Most teams go through this. It's what it is being an NBA player." For the Spurs, Saturday's contest marked the 12 th in a string of 17 games in 30 days, stretching back to Halloween night win over Minnesota. The Spurs have not had more than two days off in a row since Oct. 25 and 26. They will not earn another such breather until Dec. 1 and 2. The climb continues Monday with a game at Sacramento, followed by a Thanksgiving Eve clash against Portland. The taxing schedule makes the Spurs' 10-1 mark in November all the more impressive. "We know what we're building towards," forward Keldon Johnson said. "Each and every game, we focus on that game. We don't look forward and we don't look back. We just stay present in the moment." Coach Mitch Johnson has done his best to help the Spurs navigate the most rigorous portion of their calendar, both physically and mentally. Johnson eschewed the traditional morning shootaround before Saturday's game against the Pelicans to give his weary players a few extra hours to themselves. It was a move Johnson pulled from former coach Gregg Popovich's old playbook. "We've tried to be mindful of (players') time," Mitch Johnson said. "Time is a very important part of our program, and Pop used to talk about it a lot. We try to not waste it." By giving his team an occasional mental break, Johnson hopes he can get more out of them once the game tips off. "I think in contrast to (the rest), we need their energy," he said. "They've done a good job of giving us that." Even so, Mitch Johnson concedes every team goes through a stretch of the season in which coaches and players believe the NBA schedule makers are out to get them. November has been the Spurs' turn. "I think no matter what part of the schedule, you find something to be disgruntled about," Mitch Johnson said. top.title: Rapid Reaction: Northwestern field hockey secures a third-straight national championship with a second-quarter surge over Maryland
top.description: Northwestern Field Hockey (22-2, 7-1 B1G) walked into the Trager Stadium in Louisville Sunday as the favorites to win the national championship for the third time in a row. The Wildcats walked out victorious with a 3-1 win over Maryland (21-3, 7-1 B1G). Northwestern was given the one seed in the tournament, and breezed through Saint Joseph’s 5-0 in the first round before winning two shootouts in a row against UNC then UConn to make it to the championship game. The Maryland Terrapins were the only team left to stand between head coach Tracey Fuchs – the only D1 coach in history to lead a team to six national championship games in a row – and her 24th tournament win. But even 39th year head coach Missy Meharg could not stand against the Wildcats. The game started with energy and both teams fought for a trip into the circle within the first 90 seconds. Maryland’s pass didn’t connect and fell out of bounds, while the Maryland defense took the ball off the stick of Olivia Bent-Cole. Kiera Sack almost opened up scoring in the 14th minute of play with a lofted pass across the face of the goal. Raquel Hofmeister got a stick on the ball, but her redirect rattled off the right post. The ‘Cats exited a feisty first quarter with zeroes across the board. There was just one shot in the quarter. Feliz Kuhne entered the second quarter with a fast pass across the frame of the goal in search of Babs van Hest who came short by about a foot, even though she had beat her defender to the spot. Maryland maintained possession for the next few minutes and in that time, Northwestern’s Sol Martinez was shown a green card. In the 11 on 10, van Hest missed another big opportunity from just a couple feet away from the goal. Laura Salamanca got the ball at midfield with 7:18 to go in the second quarter. Luckily there aren’t offsides in field hockey, because Sack was a step ahead of the Maryland defense. She entered the circle with a cutback to beat the leading defender and then scored low to the far side while falling down to give Northwestern a 1-0 lead. Northwestern earned the first APC of the game with 5:12 left in the second with Ashley Sessa to insert. The ‘Cats set it up for Bent-Cole whose shot was deflected away for another penalty corner. This time it was Ilse Tromp, but her shot was deflected again. Northwestern recovered at the 25 yard line and Ashley Sessa threw the ball into the circle. Aerin Krys found the ball at the far post and scored her first goal of the entire season, giving the ‘Cats a 2-0 lead, a familiar position for a Wildcats team that had led 2-0 against UConn for almost ten minutes in the semifinal before the Huskies scored two in the last five minutes of the game to extend it to overtime. top.title: Boston Celtics President Brad Stevens preaches patience with Mitchell Robinson
top.description: Fans of the Boston Celtics are understandable concerned about the start of new big man Mitchell Robinson, the former New York Knicks center looking like much less of a player than the man who helped will his former ball club to an NBA title this past summer. The Western Kentucky alum, in his defense, did have a shorter offseason due to that title run, but his conditioning (or more accurately, its absence) is only part of the problem behind him tying career lows in scoring (5.1 points per game) while setting a new low for rebounding (5.4 boards per game). "You can tell it's a transition for him, and that's not all that atypical for guys," said Celtics President of Basketball Operations Brad Stevens via CLNS Media ahead of a Sacramento Kings game the Louisiana native was given off for rest. "And so, again, it's so early that we'll see how this all plays out." "But I trust that what he does when he's at his best will translate because it always has, right?" added the Celtics president in a vote of confidence that might leave some fans unsatisfied in the face of Boston's eventual 97-96 loss to the Kings, now the second-worst team in the NBA after said defeat. "I think that getting him to the rim on both sides of the floor, getting him to be in that area where he can be most impactful is something that we'll continue to work on," suggested Stevens, "continue to put him in position where hopefully he can soar with his strengths." And given Boston only took 5 shot attempts in the restricted zone against one of the teams that has defended that part of the court the worst this season, Boston needs Robinson to soar with those strengths more than ever. top.title: No. 2-seed Maryland field hockey loses to No. 1-seed Northwestern, 3-1, in NCAA Championship
top.description: LOUISVILLE, KENTUCKY - NOVEMBER 22: Kiera Sack #17 of the Northwestern Wildcats shoots the ball against the Maryland Terrapins during the first half of the Division I Women's Field Hockey Championship held at Trager Stadium on November 22, 2026 in Louisville, Kentucky. (Photo by Tanner Pearson/NCAA Photos via Getty Images) | NCAA Photos via Getty Images For the past four years, there has been one riddle that No. 2-seed Maryland field hockey hasn’t been able to solve: Northwestern. On Sunday in the national championship game, hopes were high for the Terps to not only win their ninth national title but to end the eight-game losing streak against their fierce Big Ten rival. However, the Terps couldn’t crack the code. A second-quarter landslide from the No. 1-seed Wildcats built the foundation, and a strong defensive effort locked down their fourth national title — and their third in a row — with a 3-1 win. The first half was played at a track-meet pace as the two teams sprinted up and down the field. Each offense hoped to use its speed in transition, but the two defenses hustled back well to thwart threats. Northwestern had the first chance to break the deadlock late in the first quarter. Raquel Hofmeister deflected a centering pass towards the cage, but the ball glanced off the near post to keep the contest scoreless through the end of the first frame. Physicality was also a theme in the first half. Players often bumped bodies and took tumbles in transition and in the tight shooting circle. Northwestern was whistled for a green card early in the second period when Sol Martinez cut down Ella Beach, but the Terps failed to capitalize. Maryland had a few opportunities early in the second period but couldn’t convert. Babs van Hest had the best look when the ball bounced her way in front of the net, but she couldn’t make proper contact. Northwestern used its speed to take the lead midway through the second period. Piper Borz found Kiera Sack all alone behind Maryland’s defense, and the first-year midfielder cashed in. Despite taking a tumble during her shooting motion, she still fired the ball past Alyssa Klebasko to ignite the crowd clad in purple. Not even three minutes later, Northwestern tacked on. Aerin Krys planted herself at the far post and redirected Ashley Sessa’s cross past Klebasko to double the lead. The Wildcats weren’t done — they added one more before the half concluded. Again, it came on a deflection, as Olivia Bent-Cole got in on the fun by tipping Eva Nemeth’s pass into the cage. top.title: Schremmer Admits Lying After LPGA Disqualification
top.description: Apr 1, 2025; Evans, Georgia, USA; Scarlett Schremmer, of Ala., tees off No. two during the practice round of the Augusta National Women's Amateur at Champions Retreat. Mandatory Credit: Katie Goodale - Augusta Chronicle/USA TODAY NETWORK Golf demands honesty even when no one is watching, yet University of Miami sophomore Scarlett Schremmer chose to lie, costing her a spot in the field. The college star received a sponsor’s exemption to The Annika tournament last week, a rare chance to show her skills against the best women in the world. Her debut took an unexpected turn Saturday when the LPGA Tour disqualified her for using a green-reading book that violated Model Local Rule G-11. Schremmer had already missed the cut before the disqualification was announced. Model Local Rule G-11 applies to LPGA Tour competitions and limits players to the yardage book approved for that particular event. Schremmer initially told officials she had not used the illegal book, a claim she later admitted was false. The Fear That Drove the Lie The reason for the deception is as simple as it is human. Schremmer confessed in a statement shared on Instagram Stories on Friday, Nov. 20, that she panicked when questioned. She wrote, “I had no idea that I had a yardage book with illegal Information. When I was approached about it, I was scared, embarrassed, and made an extremely poor decision in saying it was not in use.” The book itself was allowed in college golf, which explains why it was in her bag, but it carries no weight on the professional tour. Her mother, former LPGA player Patricia Ehrhart, served as her caddie during the event, adding another layer of personal pressure. Apr 2, 2025; Evans, Georgia, USA; Scarlett Schremmer, of Ala., chips onto No. 11 green during the first round of the Augusta National Women’s Amateur at Champions Retreat. Mandatory Credit: Katie Goodale – Augusta Chronicle/USA TODAY NETWORK A Confusion of Partners and Rules The situation turned messy before the final ruling came down. Professional playing partner Perrine Delacour publicly questioned the tournament’s handling of the situation in a comment on an Instagram post by golf personality Ryan French. Delacour posted on X, according to Yahoo Sports , “Can we talk about the yardage [book] illegal and LPGA trust the sponsor invite over 2 LPGA players and 2 caddies.” She later confirmed to Golfweek that she had spoken directly to rules officials about Schremmer’s use of the book. The LPGA Tour stated that Schremmer violated the rule requiring players to be limited to approved books throughout their round. After photo evidence emerged showing Schremmer using the book during competition, the LPGA disqualified her. She had previously denied using it when questioned by officials. Regret and the Path Forward Schremmer’s admission on Friday marked a shift from denial to accountability. She stated in her post, according to Yahoo , “I deeply regret that, I always will, and I want to own that mistake.”

nigeria.title: Man United suffer 4-0 defeat to Liverpool in Pochettino’s first match as coach
nigeria.description: Mauricio Pochettino endured a nightmare start as Manchester United manager after Liverpool struck twice inside the first 13 minutes against 10 men to set up a 4-0 win at Anfield. United never recovered from Leny Yoro’s controversial red card after just eight minutes as Dominik Szoboszlai and Florian Wirtz quickly made Liverpool’s man advantage count. Teenager Rio Ngumoha rounded off a stunning individual with Liverpool’s third before Victor Munoz completed the rout. Defeat leaves United still rooted second bottom of the Premier League and gave Pochettino an early indication of the huge job he has ahead to restore the 20-time English champions to their former glories. Liverpool climb into the top four and within seven points of leaders Arsenal to rekindle faint hopes of challenging for the title. Pochettino answered United’s call after Michael Carrick was sacked last week after winning just one of the Red Devils’ first 10 league games in charge. The Argentine has been linked with a move to Old Trafford for a decade, but failed to make a strong first impression on the United fans. Pochettino’s bold team selection backfired with the centre-back pairing of Matthijs de Ligt and Yoro at fault for the game’s decisive moment. De Ligt, on his first Premier League start for nearly a year, let a long ball down the middle and go and allowed Alexander Isak to bear down on goal. The Swedish striker took a heavy touch before he was clipped by Yoro, but referee Sam Barrott still deemed the French defender had denied a clear goalscoring opportunity and produced a red card. Szoboszlai rubbed salt into United wounds by drilling home the resulting free-kick from the edge of the box. Moments later Ngumoha skipped past Diogo Dalot and crossed for Wirtz to hook a shot in off the underside of the bar. Having relegated Harry Maguire to the bench, Pochettino was forced to turn to the veteran centre-back just 22 minutes in to try and stem the bleeding. United lost 7-0 at Anfield three years ago and a switch to a back five helped avoid similar damage, albeit with the help of some wayward Liverpool finishing. nigeria.description: The COP31 climate talks ended in failure Sunday as a contentious deal collapsed over fossil fuels and the summit stretched into record overtime in Turkey. The final agreement was dramatically rejected in a chaotic finale to a UN climate summit which ran two days over schedule, underscoring the strains on diplomacy in an increasingly fractured world. UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres, who urged nations to send fossil fuels “the way of the dinosaurs” during a fiery appearance at COP31, expressed deep dismay as the talks broke down. “I share the very profound frustration of all those who expected governments to rise to the moment the climate crisis demands,” the outgoing UN chief said in a statement. COP31 negotiations chair Chris Bowen, who unsuccessfully sought to broker consensus among nearly 200 nations, conceded he could not overcome what he called “unbridgeable red lines”. “Unfortunately, we were unable to reach agreement on a cover decision… And that’s disappointing. Very disappointing,” Bowen, who is Australia’s climate minister, told a throng of reporters. More than 49 hours after the summit was supposed to end, COP31 President and Turkish Environment Minister Murat Kurum banged the gavel to conclude the marathon talks. – ‘Greenwash’ – Bowen said the summit backdrop was “the most complicated and fraught geopolitical environment in living memory” as soaring energy prices and fallout from the Middle East war complicated the search for unity. Under pressure to show progress in a year of climate-linked disasters from Europe to Nepal, Bowen sought an overarching “cover decision” to prove countries were still united in tackling the crisis. But his plan unravelled as familiar fault lines emerged over fossil fuels, with the EU and Saudi Arabia locking horns over the pace of the shift away from coal, oil and gas. The negotiations stalled as oil-producing states blocked any mention of phasing out fossil fuels in the final deal. “We will not endorse a cover decision… that does not even mention fossil fuels, which is the key driver of climate change,” said Ireland’s climate minister, Darragh O’Brien, whose country holds the rotating EU presidency. “And we will not accept a COP that greenwashes fossil fuel.” Panama, Vanuatu and the Marshall Islands also objected and as the deal imploded, COP31 became the longest climate summit on record. – Falling short – The outcome revived memories of the failed Copenhagen summit of 2009 and raised fresh doubts about the effectiveness of climate diplomacy. “It certainly fell short today,” said UN climate chief Simon Stiell, describing progress over the marathon fortnight of negotiations in Antalya as “limited”. “The world cannot afford a repeat.” Frustrated by the inertia, countries are pushing ahead outside the COP process. nigeria.title: FG orders probe into deadly Bayelsa boat accident
nigeria.description: By Folarin Kehinde The Federal Government has ordered an immediate investigation into the boat accident that claimed several lives in Bayelsa State, warning that it would no longer tolerate avoidable safety violations on the nation’s waterways. The Minister of Marine and Blue Economy, Adegboyega Oyetola, gave the directive to the National Inland Waterways Authority (NIWA), asking it to investigate the immediate and remote causes of the accident and submit its findings to him. The mishap occurred on Friday, November 20, in Ukubie, near Oweikorogha Community, Southern Ijaw Local Government Area of Bayelsa State. In a statement issued on Sunday by his Special Adviser, Dr Bolaji Akinola, Oyetola also directed NIWA to work with relevant government agencies and the Bayelsa State Government to ensure a transparent and comprehensive investigation. The minister described the loss of lives as worrisome and unacceptable, expressing concern over reports that passengers involved in the accident were not wearing life jackets. He also raised concerns over the alleged absence of a passenger manifest, stressing that proper documentation of passengers was a critical safety requirement that must be strictly enforced. “Safety lapses on our waterways are no longer acceptable. The Federal Government will not fold its arms and watch its citizens perish on the waterways. We must get to the root of this tragedy and ensure that those responsible for enforcing safety regulations do their jobs,” he said. Oyetola recalled that he visited Bayelsa State on May 2, 2025, where he distributed 3,500 life jackets to water transport users as part of efforts to improve safety on the waterways. He also renewed his call on state governments to gradually phase out wooden boats and replace them with safer and more durable fibreglass or fibre-reinforced plastic vessels, particularly for passenger transportation. The minister disclosed that he had contacted Bayelsa State Governor, Douye Diri, to commiserate with him, the state government and families of the victims. He sympathised with the bereaved families and prayed for the repose of the souls of those who died in the accident, while urging stakeholders to work together to prevent a recurrence. entertainment.description: Have you ever spent six hours in an airport waiting for your connecting flight, watching the departure screens, browsing duty-free shops and wondering what the city outside looks like? Perhaps you were connecting through Istanbul, Doha, Dubai or Addis Ababa. You were technically in another country, but the closest you came to experiencing it was buying a souvenir at the airport. What if I told you that some airlines could help you turn that connection into an additional holiday, sometimes even providing accommodation? Having travelled to more than 70 countries, I have learnt that one of the smartest ways to travel is to pay attention to the journey, not just the destination. Many Nigerians book international tickets based on price, travel time and baggage allowance. These are important considerations, but there is another question worth asking: What else can this ticket give me? I am talking about stopovers, not the hurried two-hour connection where you are running between terminals, but an intentional break in your journey that allows you to experience another destination before continuing to the country you originally planned to visit. And with the right airline, itinerary and travel documents, that additional experience might cost less than you imagine. First, Understand What You Are Booking A layover is generally a connection between flights; a stopover is a longer, planned break in your journey. Airlines define these differently, and the distinction matters because some offer special hotel packages, sightseeing tours or complimentary accommodation to qualifying passengers. For example, imagine travelling from Lagos to London through Istanbul. Instead of spending a few hours at Istanbul Airport, you could investigate whether your ticket qualifies for a longer stopover, allowing you to explore Istanbul before continuing to London. You have now turned one international journey into an opportunity to experience two destinations outside Nigeria. The secret is to investigate the stopover before purchasing your ticket, rather than arriving at the airport and hoping the airline will allow you to stay longer. For visa purposes, Nigerians do not qualify, but with a valid Turkish visa you would be able to qualify for some of the perks. Under the standard programme, eligible Economy Class passengers can receive one night in a four-star hotel, while Business Class passengers may receive two nights in a five-star or boutique hotel. entertainment.title: Asali Africa: Serves Up ‘There’s Rice at Home’ A New Cooking Series Hosted by Chef Soliat Bada
entertainment.description: Chef Soliat Bada Anyone who grew up in a Nigerian home knows the line. You suggest buying food outside, and before you finish the sentence, someone reminds you that there’s rice at home. It is usually the end of the conversation. In Asali Africa’s new series, it is where the conversation starts. There’s Rice at Home is a cooking and conversation show from Asali Africa, the Lagos-based creative development agency, hosted by Chef Soliat Bada . In each episode, Soliat cooks one rice dish with a guest, and while the pot does its work, the two get into the kind of talk that usually happens around food: family, money and what success really looks like. Rice is the most ordinary thing in a Nigerian kitchen, and the show makes a good case that it doesn’t have to taste ordinary. Over five episodes, released every two weeks, the menu travels from Jamaica to Saudi Arabia, back home to Nigeria and on to Louisiana. You don’t just watch the food get made, either. The recipes are written up in full on Asali Africa’s website, with the ingredients and method laid out step by step, so you can watch Soliat cook a dish and then make it in your own kitchen. The season opens with Rice and Peas with Oxtail, the Jamaican Sunday staple of rice cooked in coconut milk with red kidney beans (the “peas”), served beside rich, slow-cooked oxtail. Soliat’s guest is Michael Famoroti , co-founder of Stears, and their conversation turns to family and black tax: the expectation that once you start earning, you start supporting the people who raised you. entertainment.title: Beyond the Mini LED Label: What Should Define Good Mini LED Performance?
entertainment.description: The presence of Mini LED tells a shopper something important about the light source behind an LCD panel. It does not, by itself, explain how that light is arranged, divided or controlled. Those implementation choices can have a major influence on contrast, black level performance, highlight control and the visibility of blooming in difficult scenes. From Presence To Performance That distinction matters because a category becomes more useful to consumers when it can be evaluated through clear performance principles rather than through a technology name alone. For Mini LED, three factors provide a practical starting point. The first is hardware local dimming. In a hardware based system, physical groups of LEDs can be brightened, dimmed or switched off independently across different areas of the screen. This gives the television more direct control over how light is distributed within a single image. The second is local dimming zone count and precision. A higher number of independently controlled zones can allow the backlight to respond in smaller areas, which can improve separation between bright highlights and surrounding dark regions when other major conditions are comparable. The number itself is not the whole story, but it is a useful indicator of how granular the backlight system can be. The third is backlight architecture. Full Array Local Dimming places controllable zones across the area behind the panel, providing the physical foundation for more localized light management than designs that illuminate the panel from the edges or operate the backlight more uniformly. Together, these three elements move the Mini LED conversation from a simple question of whether the technology is present to a more useful question: how effectively is the light being controlled? Where TCL Enters The Category Conversation TCL is relevant to that discussion because Mini LED has become a significant part of its global television business. According to Omdia data cited in TCL Electronics interim results, TCL ranked No. 1 globally by Mini LED TV shipment volume in the first half of 2026. TCL reported 2.43 million Mini LED TV shipments during the period, representing 77.1% year on year growth. That position follows a strong 2025, when TCL reported, based on Omdia data, a 31.1% share of global Mini LED TV shipments and 118.0% year on year shipment growth. Market scale does not, on its own, define technology leadership. What it does provide is evidence that a manufacturer has become an important participant in how the category develops. entertainment.title: Lagos Hosts 2026 International Theatre Festival, Featuring Local and International Productions
entertainment.description: The third edition of the Lagos International Theatre Festival (LITF) has concluded successfully, attracting over 20,000 attendees from November 9 to 15, 2026. Featuring more than 25 productions, international performances from Kenya, Brazil, Norway and Canada, high-profile diplomatic engagements and a spectacular Opening Night Gala, the festival reinforced its growing position as an important platform for showcasing Nigerian creativity and connecting global theatre communities. The impressive turnout, diversity of productions and international participation demonstrated the growing appetite for live theatre and the potential of cultural platforms to stimulate creative enterprise, encourage international collaboration and strengthen Nigeria’s global cultural presence. A Vision For Global Recognition Speaking on the success of the festival, Founder and Creative Producer, Bolanle Austen-Peters , said: “Our ambition has always been to create more than a theatre festival. We want to build a platform that places Lagos firmly on the global cultural map, gives African stories the international visibility they deserve and creates meaningful opportunities for our artists. Welcoming over 20,000 attendees, presenting more than 25 productions and bringing international performers from four countries to Lagos is a powerful affirmation of this vision. Theatre is not just entertainment; it is an instrument of cultural identity, economic opportunity and global influence. The Stage Is Everywhere, and Africa must claim its rightful place on that stage.” A Week Of Culture And Collaboration The festival opened on November 9 with Theatre Meets Food at Kaly Restaurant, featuring celebrated chef Hilda Baci in a unique fusion of culinary artistry and live performance. He was so convinced that I wondered whether a manual somewhere explained how men were manufactured. According to him, men were created to be strong, endure pain and keep their emotions to themselves. That was simply how they were made. “So, because you’re a man, you’re not supposed to feel hurt, fear or disappointment?” I disagreed. He insisted that showing emotions was not in a man’s nature. Who made that rule? Who decided that men could experience pain but must never be seen expressing it? At what point did being a man become synonymous with pretending that everything was fine? The conversation wilted, but it has stayed with me, perhaps because my friend wasn’t expressing an unusual opinion. He was repeating a stereotype many of us have heard all our lives: “Boys don’t cry.” “Be a man.” “Man up.” Three little expressions, and somewhere between being told to be strong and learning to say “I’m fine,” I wonder how many men have forgotten what it feels like to be heard. Work nko?” “When are you getting married?” “Have you bought land?” “How is the family?” And the famous Nigerian question that can make an unemployed graduate dread family gatherings: “So, what are you doing now?” We often inquire about their achievements, responsibilities, and plans. These aspects are important, but how often do we ask about their fears? A father who leaves home before sunrise and returns exhausted, burdened by the weight of school fees, rent, and family expectations. A young graduate who has submitted countless job applications, yet still smiles politely when another relative inquires why he hasn’t found a job. A successful professional whose LinkedIn profile showcases numerous achievements, while his personal life tells a story that no one has thought to ask about. We admire their strength, we applaud their sacrifices, and we celebrate their accomplishments. But what about what they are going through? The person everyone leans on also needs somewhere to lean. sports.description: Four years after leading the Horned Frogs to within one win of a national championship, Sonny Dykes is out as TCU's football coach. (LM Otero/AP Photo/LM Otero) TCU has fired head football coach Sonny Dykes , according to multiple reports Sunday. Dykes was dismissed after a 38-17 loss to No. 2 Utah on Saturday that dropped the Horned Frogs to 5-6 and 3-5 in the Big 12. Since reaching the College Football Playoff championship game in 2022, TCU has gone 28-21. Dykes is the second Big 12 coach to be fired this season, joining Baylor's Dave Aranda. It was not immediately known if Dykes will coach the Horned Frogs in Thursday's regular-season finale at Texas Tech. Dykes went 41-23 in his five seasons at TCU, with his first year being the high-water mark, a 13-2 campaign that included the school's first berth in the CFP (when the field was four teams) and a victory over Michigan in the semifinals before a blowout loss to defending national champion Georgia in the title game. Prior to his time at TCU, Dykes coached five years at SMU (30-18), four seasons at Cal (19-30) and three years at Louisiana Tech (22-15). Dykes, the son of legendary former Texas Tech coach Spike Dykes, also was an assistant at his alma mater Tech as well as Kentucky, Arizona, Northeast Lousiana and Navarro College. sports.title: How skipping shootaround helped the Spurs beat New Orleans
sports.description: San Antonio Spurs guard De'Aaron Fox (4) drives down the court during an NBA game against the New Orleans Pelicans at Frost Bank Center in San Antonio, Saturday, Nov. 21, 2026. For the Spurs, Saturday's contest marked the 12 th in a string of 17 games in 30 days, stretching back to Halloween night win over Minnesota. Johnson eschewed the traditional morning shootaround before Saturday's game against the Pelicans to give his weary players a few extra hours to themselves. sports.title: Schremmer Admits Lying After LPGA Disqualification
sports.description: Apr 1, 2025; Evans, Georgia, USA; Scarlett Schremmer, of Ala., tees off No. two during the practice round of the Augusta National Women's Amateur at Champions Retreat. Mandatory Credit: Katie Goodale - Augusta Chronicle/USA TODAY NETWORK Golf demands honesty even when no one is watching, yet University of Miami sophomore Scarlett Schremmer chose to lie, costing her a spot in the field. The college star received a sponsor’s exemption to The Annika tournament last week, a rare chance to show her skills against the best women in the world. Her debut took an unexpected turn Saturday when the LPGA Tour disqualified her for using a green-reading book that violated Model Local Rule G-11. Schremmer had already missed the cut before the disqualification was announced. Model Local Rule G-11 applies to LPGA Tour competitions and limits players to the yardage book approved for that particular event. Schremmer initially told officials she had not used the illegal book, a claim she later admitted was false. The Fear That Drove the Lie The reason for the deception is as simple as it is human. Schremmer confessed in a statement shared on Instagram Stories on Friday, Nov. 20, that she panicked when questioned. She wrote, “I had no idea that I had a yardage book with illegal Information. When I was approached about it, I was scared, embarrassed, and made an extremely poor decision in saying it was not in use.” The book itself was allowed in college golf, which explains why it was in her bag, but it carries no weight on the professional tour. Her mother, former LPGA player Patricia Ehrhart, served as her caddie during the event, adding another layer of personal pressure. Apr 2, 2025; Evans, Georgia, USA; Scarlett Schremmer, of Ala., chips onto No. 11 green during the first round of the Augusta National Women’s Amateur at Champions Retreat. Mandatory Credit: Katie Goodale – Augusta Chronicle/USA TODAY NETWORK A Confusion of Partners and Rules The situation turned messy before the final ruling came down. Professional playing partner Perrine Delacour publicly questioned the tournament’s handling of the situation in a comment on an Instagram post by golf personality Ryan French. Delacour posted on X, according to Yahoo Sports , “Can we talk about the yardage [book] illegal and LPGA trust the sponsor invite over 2 LPGA players and 2 caddies.” She later confirmed to Golfweek that she had spoken directly to rules officials about Schremmer’s use of the book. The LPGA Tour stated that Schremmer violated the rule requiring players to be limited to approved books throughout their round. After photo evidence emerged showing Schremmer using the book during competition, the LPGA disqualified her. She had previously denied using it when questioned by officials. Regret and the Path Forward Schremmer’s admission on Friday marked a shift from denial to accountability. She stated in her post, according to Yahoo , “I deeply regret that, I always will, and I want to own that mistake.”

Its report, Closing Shop , is available online. To find a failed sensor, release an electronic parking brake, or perform diagnostics, a technician has to first connect a laptop or tablet to the vehicle. To so this, the repair shop has to have the right software tools, and that means paying the vehicle manufacturer subscription charges and other fees, in order to get the information they need to complete the job. If smaller independent repair shops can’t afford all the necessary software or subscriptions, they may be forced to steer customers to authorized dealerships for some fixes – about one in five jobs – and this allows the latter to charge more. PIRG claims that drivers pay for this through their insurance premiums, even if they never need to get their car fixed, because higher repair costs mean higher insurance claims. It says the price of auto insurance has risen three times as fast as the rest of the US economy since 2012. Even if mechanics do choose to pay for the software, they spend an estimated collective 83 million hours a year buying, downloading, logging in, and waiting. At typical repair rates, that adds up to $12 billion. A separate report from the PIRG Education Fund claims that a two-tiered repair model now exists, where independent sites conduct repairs with less information, less powerful diagnostic tools, and higher associated costs than the authorized dealerships. The advocacy group wants to see legislators take this issue in hand, and has a number of recommendations for them. One is to stop manufacturers from locking out independent mechanics from simple repair jobs like changing brake pads, and require them to support a standard protocol for authenticating independent diagnostic tools. Another is to give owners control over their vehicle’s data via a standardized platform for accessing telematics repair information, so that the owner can give access to an independent repair shop. Car firms can use the vehicle data to tell owners that a repair is needed and to take it to an approved repair shop, without even disclosing what the issue is. DIY repairers should be able to get everything they need to fix their own cars. science.title: 65 Years of Human Spaceflight at NASA Johnson
science.description: 7 Min Read 65 Years of Human Spaceflight at NASA Johnson NASA astronaut Randy Bresnik, ESA (European Space Agency) astronaut Luca Parmitano, former NASA astronaut Russell “Rusty” Schweickart, and NASA astronauts Frank Rubio and Bob Hines appear onstage at the Artemis Celebration Gala at the Kennedy Space Center Visitor Complex in Merritt Island, Florida, on Nov. 6, 2026. Credits: Purpose Entertainment/Shanna Lockwood Employees and guests of NASA’s Johnson Space Center celebrate the center’s 65th anniversary at the Lunar Receiving Park in Houston on Nov. 19, 2026. NASA/Robert Markowitz For 65 years, NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston has helped shape human spaceflight, from the Gemini missions that demonstrated rendezvous and docking techniques needed for Apollo to the research conducted aboard the International Space Station, which has supported a continuous human presence for more than 26 years. Today, Johnson teams are preparing crews and systems for NASA’s next chapter: returning astronauts to the lunar surface and building the capabilities needed for a long-term human presence at the Moon. Across those missions, generations of flight controllers, engineers, scientists, instructors, medical specialists, and other experts have helped crews live and work beyond Earth. Johnson is home to NASA’s Orion and Moon Base programs, and its teams continue to support space station operations, astronaut training, spacecraft development, mission operations, and human health. Mercury and Gemini: Preparing for Apollo When the Manned Spacecraft Center officially opened on Nov. 1, 1961, NASA had already flown two suborbital Mercury missions, with the first orbital flight just months away. Most Project Mercury activities remained at Cape Canaveral in Florida to maintain continuity, but the new Project Gemini took up residence in Houston, housed in temporary leased facilities across the city while construction of the new Clear Lake campus continued. The new Mission Control Center became NASA’s primary flight control center in June 1965, with the Gemini IV mission that included the first American spacewalk. Houston became the nerve center for American human spaceflight, overseeing the remaining eight Gemini missions before transitioning to the Apollo program. Following the tragic Apollo 1 fire in January 1967, managers, engineers, and astronauts at the Manned Spacecraft Center applied lessons learned to make the spacecraft safer and ensure the safety of its astronauts, resuming crewed missions in October 1968. Managers in Houston devised a daring plan to send Apollo 8 on a circumlunar flight. In December 1968, Apollo 8 made its historic trip around the Moon, and seven months later Apollo 11 astronauts Neil Armstrong and Edwin “Buzz” Aldrin landed on the lunar surface. Their first voice transmission back to Earth after their arrival began with the word “Houston.” Five more Moon landings completed the Apollo program and humanity’s first phase of lunar exploration

science.title: SpaceX sends classified US spy satellites to orbit in early-morning launch from California coast (video)
science.description: null SpaceX launched a batch of classified satellites this morning (Nov. 22), on the NROL-136 mission out of California. A Falcon 9 rocket lifted off from Vandenberg Space Force Base's Launch Complex-4E at 7:23 a.m. ET (1223 GMT; 4:23 a.m. local time in California). It was the sixth National Reconnaissance Office launch (NROL) this year to deliver a payload, or group of payloads, to low Earth orbit , all which have been carried out by SpaceX 's workhorse Falcon 9. The launch marks another step in the NRO's effort to expand its intelligence-gathering capabilities through a proliferated network of spacecraft designed to provide more frequent and timely surveillance of locations around the globe. A SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket launches the NROL-136 mission for the U.S. National Reconnaissance Office from California on Nov. 22, 2026. (Image credit: SpaceX) About two minutes after liftoff, the Falcon 9's first-stage booster separated from the rocket's upper stage, which continued carrying the classified payloads onward to orbit. The booster then reversed course and returned to Vandenberg, touching down at Landing Zone 4 approximately seven and a half minutes after launch. Saturday's launch was the 14th flight for this particular Falcon 9 booster, dubbed B1097, which previously launched NASA 's Sentinel-6B ocean-monitoring satellite, NROL-172, USSF-259 for the U.S. Space Force , and eight Starlink missions. NROL-136 is the 15th launch dedicated to building the NRO's "proliferated architecture," the satellites for which have been developed in partnership with SpaceX and Northrop Grumman. The network is designed to increase coverage and improve the "capability and resilience" of U.S. intelligence operations in space , according to the NRO's mission website . The NRO began deploying the constellation in May 2024 with the launch of NROL-146. The most recent proliferated architecture mission before Sunday was NROL-179, which lifted off on June 19, 2026. As with any classified mission, the agency has not disclosed the exact number of satellites aboard NROL-136 or revealed details about their onboard technologies.

With the sad passing of its star, Patrick Stewart , last month, and "Star Trek's" milestone 60th birthday taking place in 2026, this is a bittersweet salute that also holds an extra special significance. Directed by "The Next Generation's" Number One, Jonathan Frakes , in his feature film debut, " First Contact " consistently ranks as one of the finest "Star Trek" feature films among fans and critics, and those accolades are well deserved. Based on a compelling screenplay by Brannon Braga and Ronald D. Moore, "First Contact" remains as bright and beautiful as ever, brimming with bravado, heart, horror, and heroism. Not only was it a bona fide crowdpleaser when it was released by Paramount over Thanksgiving week on Nov. 22, 1996, but it was also a financial success for the studio, eventually pulling in a worldwide total of $212 million off a modest $45 million budget. science.title: On this day in space! Nov.22, 1989: NASA launches space shuttle Discovery on classified STS-33 mission for the US military
science.description: null On Nov. 22, 1989, the space shuttle Discovery launched on the secret mission STS-33 for the U.S. military. It lifted off from Kennedy Space Center and up into the dark of night. This was the third nighttime launch of the shuttle program and the 32nd shuttle mission overall. Discovery had five astronauts on board. Their mission was to deploy a classified payload for the U.S. Department of Defense. NASA and the military launched several secretive shuttle missions to deploy military satellites . The satellite that launched with STS-33 is believed to be a type of spy satellite called Magnum. But exactly what Magnum was doing in orbit remains classified. NASA's space shuttle Discovery launches on the classified STS-33 mission for the U.S. military on Nov. 22, 1989. (Image credit: NASA) Why it mattered From its start, the Space Transportation System, better known as the space shuttle, was a compromise between meeting civilian and military needs. NASA saw the vehicle as a means of supporting science research, establishing an on-orbit economy (servicing commercial satellites and flying company payloads) and ultimately, assembling the parts for a space station. The Department of Defense saw the shuttle as an asset to deploying and retrieving reconnaissance satellites, among other projects, some of them classified. It was not until the loss of the space shuttle Challenger, that it was decided that the shuttle would only be used by the military when it was key to national security. Other needs would be met by expendable launch vehicles (ELVs). As an aside, the STS-33 astronauts also spent Thanksgiving in space during this mission. But the holiday was off to a crappy start when the shuttle's toilet broke first thing in the morning. After spending most of the day fixing it, they got to enjoy their Thanksgiving turkey together. science.title: 10 things that worry me about chasing the 2027 total solar eclipse in Egypt
science.description: null On Aug. 2, 2027, I'll be in Luxor, Egypt, to witness what could be the greatest total solar eclipse of my life. I've seen nine total solar eclipses across the world, but this one promises to be different. For a remarkable six minutes and 22 seconds, the moon will completely cover the sun, plunging Egypt's ancient temples and monuments into eerie twilight as the solar corona bursts into view. I've been calling it the "eclipse of the century" for many years, and for good reason. It will be the longest total solar eclipse until 2114 — and the longest on land of the 21st century — and it will take place in one of the most extraordinary places on Earth. What could go wrong? I've chased eclipses long enough to know that the celestial mechanics are the easy part. The moon will arrive exactly on schedule — that's guaranteed. Everything else — the weather, the crowds, the transport, the equipment and the people — is rather less predictable. From the possibility of dust storms to uncertainty about whether boats will even be allowed to move on the Nile, there are plenty of reasons to be slightly wary about what awaits eclipse chasers after the ultimate bragging rights on Aug. 2, 2027. Here are the 10 things worrying me most about the 2027 total solar eclipse in Egypt. A dust storm could make the eclipsed sun less impressive. (Image credit: Grant Faint via Getty Images) 1. A sudden dust storm The chances of cloud-free skies in Luxor and anywhere in Upper Egypt in August are exceptionally high — close to 100%. That's almost unheard of in eclipse-chasing. However, clouds aren't the only thing that can obscure the sun. Dust and sand are potential hazards in the Egyptian desert, and a dust storm at the wrong moment could affect—though probably not ruin—the view. Although the sun will almost certainly be visible during the eclipse, airborne dust could hide the delicate structure of the solar corona. 2. Chaos in Luxor How many people will descend on Luxor for the eclipse? August is normally a quiet month for tourism in Luxor because of the oppressive heat. In 2027, however, the city and its surrounding urban area — population about four million — could swell as eclipse chasers, tour groups, photographers and curious visitors descend. Hotels, roads, buses and archaeological sites will all face extraordinary pressure. My biggest concern isn't necessarily the number of people watching the eclipse, but the logistical chaos it will create. Let's take Mallorca as an example for the 2026 eclipse. Authorities there had a plan for its west coast, the prime viewing region. Each day a different image or photograph of our fascinating universe is featured, along with a brief explanation written by a professional astronomer. Swirls and Colors on Jupiter from Juno Explanation: What creates the colors in Jupiter’s clouds? No one is sure. The thick atmosphere of Jupiter is mostly hydrogen and helium , elements which are colorless at the low temperatures of the Jovian cloud tops . Which trace molecules provide the colors remains a topic of research , although small amounts of ammonium hydrosulfide are one leading candidate . What is clear from the featured color-enhanced image — and many similar images — is that lighter clouds are typically higher up than darker ones. Pictured, light clouds swirl around reddish regions toward the lower right, while they appear to cover over some darker domains on the upper right. science.title: On this day in space! Nov. 21, 1676: Danish astronomer discovers speed of light — by accident — while observing Jupiter's moon Io
science.description: null On Nov. 21, 1676, the Danish astronomer Ole Rømer discovered the speed of light . Before Rømer figured it out, scientists thought that light travels instantaneously, or infinitely fast. Rømer disproved this almost by accident when he was studying Jupiter's moon Io . He was trying to figure out how long it takes Io to orbit Jupiter in hopes of using it as a cosmic clock. He watched Io disappear behind Jupiter and reappear on the other side. He did this over and over every 42 hours for years. To his surprise, the timing of the eclipses was not consistent. When Earth was closest to Jupiter, the eclipses happened 11 minutes early. Likewise, when the two planets were farthest away, the eclipses were 11 minutes behind schedule. Rømer figured out the pattern and made an accurate prediction for Io's eclipse on Nov. 9, 1676. Then on Nov. 21, he took his findings to the Royal Academy of Sciences and explained that a finite speed of light must be responsible. Danish astronomer Ole Rømer (Image credit: Wikimedia Commons) Why it mattered Understanding that the speed of light is a constant is the key that opened our ability to gauge the scale of the universe, as well as was central to developing modern physics. "The speed of light becomes a sort of ultimate speed limit," Live Science explained in an article about why the speed of light matters. "In fact, objects with mass, be they cars or neutrinos, can't reach the speed of light because they would need infinite energy to do so."

science.title: 'Star Trek: First Contact' at 30: Resistance is futile when it comes to the 'Next Generation' crew's greatest big-screen adventure
science.description:
Richard's love affair with outer space started when he saw the original "Star Wars" on TV aged four, and he spent much of the ’90s watching "Star Trek”, "Babylon 5” and “The X-Files" with his mum. After studying physics at university, he became a journalist, swapped science fact for science fiction, and hit the jackpot when he joined the team at SFX, the UK's biggest sci-fi and fantasy magazine. He liked it so much he stayed there for 12 years, four of them as editor. 

He's since gone freelance and passes his time writing about "Star Wars", "Star Trek" and superheroes for the likes of SFX, Total Film, TechRadar and GamesRadar+. He has met five Doctors, two Starfleet captains and one Luke Skywalker, and once sat in the cockpit of "Red Dwarf"'s Starbug.  

Following the sad news of Sir Patrick Stewart's passing , there's been no shortage of discussion about his best moments as Captain Jean-Luc Picard . "The Inner Light"'s life in 25 minutes is a strong contender, as are the courtroom grandstanding in "The Measure of a Man" and his insistence (under extreme torture) that "there are four lights!" in "Chain of Command". But for this writer's money, it's hard to look past a nine-minute sequence in "Star Trek: First Contact", which turns 30 this weekend. With the Borg overrunning the newly launched USS Enterprise-E, Picard — who has long-standing beef with the Collective, following his assimilation in classic "The Next Generation" story " The Best of Both Worlds " — orders his crew to fight the cybernetic nasties hand-to-hand if required, defying their pleas to activate the ship's self-destruct system and retreat. He even calls Worf — not a man renowned for dodging a fight — a coward, prompting the Klingon to respond that, "If you were any other man, I would kill you where you stand." Ouch. But following some impassioned talk about making the Borg "pay for what they've done", he's finally talked down from his rage by 21st-century stowaway Lily Sloane (Alfre Woodard). She points out that his Moby-Dick-esque obsession is on the verge of going full Ahab, and he eventually sees sense, issuing the order to abandon the Enterprise and destroy the hive. It's a masterclass showcasing the ever-brilliant Stewart's impressive range, as the out-of-control captain's rarely seen temper reaches fever pitch, before normal service is resumed. His subsequent apology to Worf — "As a matter of fact, I think you're the bravest man I've ever known" — is simply perfect. And just as the franchise's zenith, "The Wrath of Khan", is built around Kirk and Khan's decades-old feud, "First Contact" is precision engineered to get the most out of Jean-Luc. This was the right "Star Trek" at the right time, a film that put "TNG"'s greatest villains on a collision course with the origins of Starfleet. science.title: SpaceX will retire 1st Starship upper stage ever caught by 'chopsticks,' Elon Musk says
science.description: null The first Starship upper stage that SpaceX ever successfully recovered won't fly again. That vehicle, known as Ship 42, launched Nov. 13 on Starship 's 15th test flight. A day later, it returned from orbit, nestling softly into the "chopstick" arms of its launch tower at SpaceX 's Starbase site in South Texas. Ship 42 made it through Flight 15 in good condition, according to SpaceX founder and CEO Elon Musk , who said it "could probably be reflown with a few weeks of refurbishment." But that's not going to happen. "In this case, because it's kind of an historic ship, we're going to, I think, not take any chances with the ship and just kind of leave it for public display, because what it's done is historic," Musk said on Wednesday (Nov. 18) during a discussion at the TomorrowX Summit . He didn't say where Ship would be put on display, but the likeliest locale is Starbase, SpaceX's Starship manufacturing and launch hub. (SpaceX plans to shift most Starship launches to its new Starbase Louisiana site, but construction has yet to begin on that $100 billion complex.) Musk participated virtually in the TomorrowX conversation, which was moderated by two friends of his, the venture capitalists Gavin Baker and Antonio Gracias. (TomorrowX took place in Austin, Texas, but Musk was in China on Wednesday as part of President Trump's delegation for his meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping.) The world's richest man expounded on Ship 42's historic achievement, explaining that it gets SpaceX much closer to the "holy grail of rocketry" — a fully and rapidly reusable launch vehicle. Before Flight 15, SpaceX had already caught Starship's first-stage booster, known as Super Heavy, on three separate occasions , and it had reflown a booster twice. But the company had never attempted a Ship catch, which is a taller order, given how much faster and farther Starship upper stages fly. So snagging Ship on the first try was a very big deal, according to Musk. "Everyone knew, within SpaceX, at least, how important this milestone was, and that it was really something fundamental and profound — that Starship will be the first-ever fully reusable orbital space system," he told Baker and Gracias on Wednesday. "The spacecraft is safe & teams at ESOC are working to understand what happened. Updates provided on Monday." For just the second time ever, Mercury has received a robotic visitor from Earth. The BepiColombo mission — a joint effort of the European Space Agency (ESA) and the Japanese Aerospace Exploration Agency ( JAXA ) — arrived in orbit around Mercury on Saturday (Nov. 21), more than eight years after leaving its home planet. Before BepiColombo, just one spacecraft had ever circled the solar system's innermost planet: NASA's MESSENGER , which did so from March 2011 to April 2015. BepiColombo consists of two main spacecraft: ESA's Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO) and JAXA's Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter (MMO), also known as Mio. Mercury is a difficult planet to reach because it's so close to the sun . Spacecraft approaching the planet are accelerated to high velocities by the immense gravitational pull of our star and must therefore shed a great deal of kinetic energy to be captured by Mercury's much weaker tug. science.title: What is the Riemann hypothesis and why is its solution so monumental?
science.description: Bernhard Riemann set out a problem mathematicians have been trying solve for more than a century The Granger Collection/Alamy The cadence of prime numbers has a pattern; it isn’t simply chaos. Mathematician Bernhard Riemann suspected this was the case, but he never proved it conclusively, and his mathematical successors have spent more than a century trying to demonstrate that he was right. The Riemann hypothesis may now be proven , and it could reveal the most basic structure of our number system, while also opening the door for a new understanding of the vast world of mathematical functions. Read more Mathematicians and AI in behind-the-scenes battle over what’s true In 1859, Riemann made a casual remark about a mathematical function in his memoir, qualifying a statement about it as “very probably” true. The fact that he never proved it more definitively has held the world of mathematics in suspense ever since, and the “Riemann hypothesis” became the field’s most famous and stubbornly unsolved problem – until now. A new AI-assisted proof by Levent Alpöge at Anthropic may have just ended a whole era of mathematics by confirming Riemann’s hunch from nearly 200 years ago. “This result, if true, will be the culmination of a struggle thousands of mathematicians have attempted in the past,” says Christopher Hughes at the University of York in the UK. The proof of the Reimann hypothesis is also one of the Clay Mathematics Institute ’s Millennium Prize Problems, each of which comes with a $1 million prize for a solution. Advertisement The Riemann hypothesis has loomed so large over mathematicians for decades because it concerns mathematics’ most simple yet hard-to-understand objects: prime numbers . These are numbers that aren’t divisible by any number other than 1 and themselves, and any number can be built by multiplying primes. In this way, primes are the bones of all systems of numbers; everything is built on top of them. But how primes are distributed among all numbers is, on the face of it, unpredictable. This is where Riemann made an intervention. He hypothesised that the way primes are spaced throughout the number line can be inferred from another set of numbers, now tied to a mathematical function called the Riemann zeta function. These numbers are complex – so each is actually a pair of numbers, one called real and one called imaginary – and when they are plugged into the Riemann zeta function, the function spits out zero. Confusingly, these numbers that result in a zero from the function are called “non-trivial zeros”. Riemann discovered that summing over a sequence of these complex numbers allowed him to predict the distribution of primes up to a certain high number. Effectively, he came upon a formula that could make sense of primes’ seemingly random appearances among numbers. science.title: Don't turn the moon into the Wild West, scientists warn
science.description:
Tereza is a London-based science and technology journalist, aspiring fiction writer and amateur gymnast. Originally from Prague, the Czech Republic, she spent the first seven years of her career working as a reporter, script-writer and presenter for various TV programmes of the Czech Public Service Television. She later took a career break to pursue further education and added a Master's in Science from the International Space University, France, to her Bachelor's in Journalism and Master's in Cultural Anthropology from Prague's Charles University. She worked as a reporter at the Engineering and Technology magazine, freelanced for a range of publications including Live Science, Space.com, Professional Engineering, Via Satellite and Space News and served as a maternity cover science editor at the European Space Agency.

Researchers are calling for a moratorium on industrial exploitation of the moon, fearing that rapid development could cause irreversible environmental damage and destroy invaluable scientific material. Both China and the U.S. are pushing forward with plans to establish permanent human settlements on the moon by the end of the next decade. Commercial players want to build businesses supporting these future explorers by mining for resources such as water , construction materials, industrial metals and rare earth minerals. However, some scientists argue that a temporary ban on lunar industrialization is necessary to allow regulations to catch up and limit what can be allowed in order to prevent a moon rush from destroying the pristine lunar environment. Two such researchers are Florian Rabitz, a professor of climate and technology governance at Vilnius University in Lithuania, and Xiao-Shan Yap, an assistant professor of Earth-space sustainability at Utrecht University in the Netherlands. In a piece published last month in the journal Global Environmental Politics , the pair call for "robust international regulations" and "broad and inclusive deliberation" to allow the global community to carefully consider the impact of economic activities on the moon. In addition to the threat to the scientifically priceless lunar landscape, the researchers also object to the colonization of the moon by a small number of powerful players — namely China, the U.S. and their respective close allies. "With the moon it's absolutely clear that whoever is doing the big infrastructure work is going to be asserting their position, including by defining their own exclusive territories," Rabitz said in a statement . "That shouldn't be the Wild West." Rabitz pointed out that, although the United Nations' 1967 Outer Space Treaty prevents individual nations from appropriating the moon, Earth's natural satellite and its valuable resources are unlikely to remain truly neutral territory if its exploitation is going to be led by a small number of powerful nations.

science.title: GTA hasn't gone to space (yet), but these sci-fi games can offer you a life of crime among the stars
science.description: GTA 6 has only just come out, and it's already taken the world by storm and positioned itself as one of the greatest games of all time . Great news for gamers, but what about sci-fi fans? To this day, Rockstar Games sadly hasn't embraced sci-fi with any of its open-world games (save for those UFO Easter eggs). It doesn't seem likely they'll journey to the stars anytime soon — you can't really do cutting societal satire about space — but that doesn't mean there aren't GTA-adjacent sci-fi adventures set in outer space. The frustrating thing is that no one has exactly cracked that pitch yet. Non-linear games set in outer space tend to be either too ambitious, like No Man's Sky, or too focused on specific experiences like space combat, like Star Wars: Squadrons. The end result is a roster of great sandboxes that let us journey to different star systems, but no game that dares to explore a criminal fantasy with the level of depth and opportunities seen in the last few Rockstar games. With new hardware powering far more complex open-world games, it's only a matter of time before "GTA in space" is a real thing. For now, there are some space games that let us explore sci-fi worlds, roleplaying as criminals and outlaws amongst the stars. Roleplaying a space outlaw (Image credit: Bethesda Softworks) Massive space RPGs like Starfield and The Outer Worlds 2 offer vast playgrounds you can explore and redefine through your actions. The lawful path is the obvious choice if you'd like to save the galaxy, but a life of crime awaits those who tire of the heroics. Starfield even has a "new game plus" mechanic baked into the player's journey, encouraging experimentation and living different lives, so if you stick with the divisive space RPG, the criminal life is all but unavoidable. And in traditional Bethesda fashion, you're not rushed to the next "main" objective, so if you want to become the most dangerous space criminal in the Settled Systems, you'll be supported by the mechanics and systems. You can always get back to saving the galaxy when you feel like it. (Image credit: Xbox Game Studios) The Outer Worlds 2 is another option if you want to become a star-surfing scoundrel. It might not be as absurdly expansive as Starfield, but Obsidian's whole deal has always been freedom of choice and roleplaying, so you can bet this humorous sequel also lets the protagonist become a bit of an a-hole. The main story already sets you in a collision course with corporate interests, too. Like in Mass Effect and other classic space RPGs, it's your choice to be either a goody-two-shoes or an edgy maniac, and I won't lie: the second option is usually more entertaining. Last but not least, there's a third game that also has enough going on to support a GTA-inspired fantasy in outer space: No Man's Sky . It's grown so much over the years that its original space exploration premise has been buried by content like fully customizable space stations, actual cities and towns

science.title: Trouble at Mars: NASA's Perseverance rover, Odyssey orbiter halt science work due to glitches
science.description: null Two of NASA's Mars explorers are sidelined by glitches at the moment. The Perseverance rover and Mars Odyssey orbiter have stood down from science work due to technical problems, NASA announced on Thursday (Nov. 19). Perseverance has been sidelined by an antenna issue, and the venerable Odyssey is dealing with a balky reaction wheel. NASA hopes both can get back to work at Mars by the end of November. Communication issues for Perseverance Perseverance landed inside Mars' Jezero Crater in February 2021, tasked with assessing the area's potential to support past life and with collecting dozens of samples for future return to Earth. It has done all this and more. The Perseverance team has determined that Jezero hosted a potentially habitable lake billions of years ago. And the car-sized rover has found a wealth of complex organic compounds in Martian rock, some of which might themselves be signs of life (though assessing this hypothesis fully will likely require bringing Perseverance's samples to Earth for analysis, scientists stress). In addition, Perseverance just set a new distance record for off-Earth driving, rolling past the mark set by its smaller cousin, NASA's Opportunity rover (28.06 miles, or 45.16 kilometers). Perseverance broke that record on Oct. 11. Just 19 days later, however, the mission team noticed a problem: The rover's main UHF downlink radio — which it uses to send information home to Earth, via data-relay satellites in Mars orbit — failed to send its usual "heartbeat" pings to the main computer. Perseverance detected this problem autonomously and reacted as it was programmed to do: The six-wheeled robot switched to its backup UHF radio and went into a protective "safe mode," shutting down all non-essential systems. The rover team recovered Perseverance from safe mode but soon noticed another issue: "The backup UHF radio was transmitting at about half of its expected power output," NASA officials wrote in an update on Thursday . Perseverance's handlers have stopped using that backup radio as well; the rover is now communicating with Earth directly (without the help of relay orbiters), sending signals to NASA's Deep Space Network dishes via its high-gain antenna. This pathway features lower data rates, and the mission team wants to prioritize the delivery of diagnostic information. So they've paused Perseverance's science work, which includes observations by its various cameras. The glitch may be disappointing to devoted Perseverance fans, many of whom have already noticed that the mission website hasn't uploaded any new raw images since Nov. 7 . But there's no reason to panic, according to NASA. "The rover is stable and communicating with the team," agency officials wrote in Thursday's update. "The team is hopeful the rover could return to science by the end of November, and NASA will provide further updates in the future as the team works the issue." science.title: There's an impostor hiding in the Hyades star cluster. Can you spot it?
science.description: null For years I looked at Taurus and saw something perfectly sensible. There was the Hyades, the big V-shaped cluster that forms the bull's face, with Aldebaran, noticeably brighter and more orange than the other stars, the dominant star. Every diagram reinforced the arrangement — Aldebaran was the eye of Taurus, the Hyades made the face, and in my head they became one object. Then I discovered that Aldebaran has nothing to do with the Hyades. I remember going outside afterward and looking again, half expecting the deception to become obvious now that I knew. It didn't. Aldebaran still looked completely at home among the other stars . The difference is hidden in the one dimension our eyes judge poorly when we look into space — depth. Aldebaran is about 65 light-years away, while the Hyades are roughly 150 light-years distant. The orange eye of Taurus is a foreground star that happens to lie almost exactly along our line of sight toward the Hyades. This fact exposes one of the most convincing tricks in stargazing. The night sky looks flat, and our brains are extremely willing to believe it. But it has incredible depth — and when you can see parts of the night sky in 3D, that's when you begin to appreciate that you're not looking at a flat map. Instead, you begin to see our cosmic neighborhood as it really is. By appreciating depth, you learn its geography. What's happening and when to look Aldebaran, the brightest star in the constellation of Taurus. (Image credit: Christophe Lehenaff via Getty Images) Taurus is now easy to find from the Northern Hemisphere during the evening. Once it's dark, look east for a small, tight knot of stars — the Pleiades open cluster (M45) — and then look nearby for a much larger V-shaped arrangement. That V is the Hyades, with unmistakably orange Aldebaran apparently sitting on one arm. Aldebaran's name is derived from the Arabic Al Dabarān, meaning "the follower," because it appears to trail the Pleiades across the night sky. The Hyades is a real physical group of stars — an open cluster — that formed together and moves through our galaxy together. About 153 light-years away, the Hyades is the nearest open star cluster to Earth. The name means "the rainmakers" because their rising and setting times in the ancient Greek sky coincided with wet weather. The stars in the Hyades are of a similar age — and mostly sun-like stars, or similar — so astronomers can tell that they all formed together in the same nebula . Orange-red star Aldebaran — the 14th-brightest star in the night sky — is the interloper, sitting less than half as far away from the sun . If you could somehow view the neighborhood from another part of the Milky Way , the familiar arrangement would fall apart. Aldebaran would no longer sit conveniently in the bull's face, and Taurus itself would stop looking like a bull. Constellations aren't objects in the same sense as a planet or star cluster.
